words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The plural verb follows the generic sense of singular alladhī, whose reference is a class of spenders; Arabic can shift from singular form to plural meaning.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The inability clause can be independent or circumstantial; one objection says the intervening parable bars a circumstantial link, while al-Samīn treats the parable as a reinforcing parenthesis.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The inability clause is deliberately flexible: a state of the spenders or figurative rock, an explanatory resumption, a summary, or a state with an omitted relative pronoun.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The wording uses ellipsis by correspondence: neither the represented giver nor the example's planter has any gain.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The plural pronoun may instead refer back to the believers addressed by the command, by a shift from direct address to third person.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The plural pronoun can refer to show-offs, disbelievers, and donors who reproach recipients as the group unable to benefit from its deeds.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: The image may supply a generic subject: no one can recover seed from soil washed off bare rock; likewise the donor cannot recover benefit from the deed.
Reminding a recipient of a gift or hurting the recipient nullifies that charity's reward.
note: Some notes compare this loss with showy spending; Ibn Zayd says the whole gift is erased and cites 2:270 and 2:272.

view: Nullification affects the charity's reward, not the completed physical act.
Only the gift's excellence or favorable effect in the recipient's heart is lost through reproach; a sincere giver's original reward remains, whereas the show-off receives no reward.
note: Qurṭubī prefers the first account in his reported disagreement.

view: Reproach stops the gift's future multiplication, but preserves reward earned before the reproach.
The verse warns that reproach and harm can match or outweigh charity's reward, effectively nullifying it.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: At judgment, showy or harmful givers cannot obtain reward or other benefit from what they spent, just as no soil or harvest remains on the stone.

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
view: A further sense is that they fail to put their earnings where they belong, spending without effect for the afterlife.
The point about language and interpretation is transmitted from exegetes even where they did not summarize it expressly under charity's nullification.
Sins do not generally erase good deeds; this warning concerns the particular gift that is not accepted, without nullifying unrelated good acts.
A gift from a donor whom God knows will later reproach or harm is never accepted as charity, so no earned reward is subsequently erased.
note: Disputed by the account that reproach removes reward already earned.

view: God marks the recording angel not to write down a gift whose donor will later reproach or harm.
Later reproach or harm removes reward that charity had already earned.
note: The opposing account says corrupt intention made the gift invalid from its beginning.

view: The command can mean that donors must not perform a gift in a null form: ostentation or anticipated reproach shows its intention was corrupt and it never acquired reward.
note: Al-Ālūsī notes that this reading departs from the apparent wording.

view: A later event cannot erase an earlier earned merit: distinct merits do not conflict, and if they did, neither would have priority; prevention of reward is easier than reversal.
Explaining a prior merit's disappearance by a later event is circular, since that event could act only once prior resistance had already disappeared.
Abū Hāshim's mutual balancing of merit and fault is rejected because reciprocal erasure would require both causes simultaneously to exist and not exist.
Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī says later punishment alone cancels earlier reward; al-Rāzī objects that this leaves earlier good without benefit, against justice and the promise of 99:7.
Al-Jubbāʾī says eternal pure reward and eternal pure punishment cannot both be deserved, because one outcome would then be both just punishment and unjust denial of reward.
A minor sin cannot cancel arbitrary equal portions of reward; canceling all reward is rejected by agreement, so it cancels none.
A major punishment cannot cancel earlier reward by an arbitrarily selected portion, while making every portion independently cancel it yields impossible multiple causes of one effect.
Good and blameworthy consequences can coexist without canceling each other, as a servant can deserve praise for saving his master and blame for exposing his property to theft.
The Muʿtazilite claim that one grave sin can outweigh decades of obedience because disobeying a generous God is so grave is rejected as unjust; faith can also erase long unbelief.
Reward is God's gift rather than an automatic entitlement; boasting turns a God directed loan or transaction into a gift aimed at the recipient and reveals emptiness from the outset.
For voluntary charity, lost reward leaves the gift as though never made; for obligatory alms, loss of reward threatens the giver as though the duty were unfulfilled.
The text moves from spending in God's path to gifts to needy individuals, where donor and recipient know each other and reminders or injury are more likely.
The passage organizes giving by purpose, manner, quality of wealth, recipient, and reward; its connected themes suggest revelation as one unit.
The warning against harm precedes the positive incentive because averting harm takes priority, then returns to boasting and ostentation with a clearer image.
Mann is recalling or boasting of a favor to the recipient, claiming credit for a gift.
Arabic idiom calls a gift used for reproach a black hand, an unsolicited gift a white hand, and a requested gift a green hand.
Believers are addressed directly and the warning repeated to strengthen avoidance of reproach and harm, which are especially ugly in charity.
Reproach is directed toward God for the donor's gift, while injury is directed toward the person receiving or requesting it.
note: Others direct both actions toward the recipient.

view: Both reproach and injury are directed toward the poor recipient; this is presented as the clearer or majority reading.
A soldier who curses his commander and campaign after hardship and vows not to return may forfeit credit for his jihad spending, analogously to a gift spoiled by reproach.

A Prophetic warning lists the habitual drinker, disobedient child, and reproacher of gifts among those barred from Paradise; Ibn ʿAbbās was troubled, then found verses addressing these sins and allowing repentance.
A Prophetic report says God will not look at a person who reproaches recipients, alongside the parent abuser and habitual drinker.
A Prophetic report says reminding others of a favor erases gratitude and reward, then recites this verse; no grading is stated.
A transmitted Prophetic statement says a person who does a believer a favor and then verbally hurts or reminds him has nullified that charity.
Qatāda says God dislikes reproach and harm for believers.
Keeping wealth is better than giving it and then following the gift with reminders or harm.
Counting favors aloud destroys the good of beneficence and gratitude; admiring one's own deed destroys its reward.
Mālik disliked giving obligatory alms to relatives lest their praise, reminders, or repayment taint the gift; he favored strangers or an intermediary when the ruler was unjust.
Reminding the poor person shows the giver sought the recipient rather than God; one seeking God would feel indebted to the poor person as a means of reaching Him.
A hadith that the rich would perish without the poor is read to mean that poor recipients provide the rich a path to God.
One reading reverses 'the upper hand is better': the poor person's is higher because the rich donor gives through the poor and receives spiritual benefit.
Adhā is reproaching, rebuking, or otherwise hurting the recipient.
The showy spender denies God's oneness and lordship, resurrection, and recompense, revealing a hypocrite.
The giver seeks neither charity's reward nor safety from punishment for withholding it.
The show-off's denial concerns belief in God's call to spend and its promised Judgment reward in this deed, rather than disbelief in God altogether.
note: This differs from the reading that identifies the spender as a hypocrite or unbeliever.

view: In an inward reading, harm is turning to anything other than the Real, corrupting devotion mixed with worldly or even otherworldly motives.
The comparison's kāf can describe an omitted verbal noun: do not invalidate charity with invalidation like the show-off's, or do not spend like his spending.
The kāf can instead be accusative as a circumstantial description of the addressed donors: do not nullify gifts while resembling a showy spender.
The showy spender is a hypocrite who outwardly presents a faithful deed but inwardly seeks praise rather than God or the afterlife; ostentation fits hidden disbelief.
note: A rival reading allows an openly unbelieving spender.

view: The spender may be an openly unbelieving person who seeks public praise for generosity.
note: Others prefer a hypocrite because concealed disbelief makes the display religiously deceptive.

view: The relative expression denotes a generic class of ostentatious spenders, not one particular person.
A showy giver spends to be seen as generous, good, or pious and win human praise, with no intention of God's approval or reward.
note: The STUDY key is corrected in the final mapping.

view: Believers who reproach or harm are likened to showy spenders because both lack sincere God directed giving; this warns against ostentation as a trait of disbelievers.
The show-off's worthless spending is the clearer case against which harmful giving is compared.
The comparison vilifies harmful giving without making every legal ruling for a showy unbeliever apply to the believer.
Riyāʾ means displaying a deed to people so they see and praise it; the word is derived from seeing.
Riyāʾ is a verbal noun with a reciprocal or intensive form: the giver displays deeds and people respond with praise; its forms are analyzed from seeing.
Riyāʾ can be parsed as the purpose of spending, as a circumstantial state or manner, or as qualifying an omitted verbal noun.
Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif, also transmitted from ʿĀṣim and others, eases the first hamza of riyāʾ to yāʾ after kasra without changing meaning.
A report says ostentation is the lesser shirk feared for the community; at judgment show-offs are told to seek recompense from those whose notice they sought.
A hadith recounts a wealthy donor who sought to be called generous; he receives the praise he wanted but no reward from God.
The report also condemns a warrior seeking to be called brave and a scholar or reciter seeking fame; they are among the first judged and cast into Hell.
ʿAbd Allāh al-Madanī's report is introduced through a man asking Abū Hurayrah why he repeatedly wept while narrating the Prophet's warning.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Zakariyyā heard that showing off in one deed can cancel what came before it.
Early donors concealed charity by seeking blind recipients, attaching money to a sleeping poor person's clothing, or leaving it for a poor person to find.
Ostentation can mean acting heedless of God's seeing while concentrating on people's gaze.
Giving merely to be seen is presented as the worst model of charity, as in the Quranic warning about ostentatious worshippers.
A reported analogy compares ostentatious worship with carrying a sack full of stones: observers praise its fullness, but it buys nothing.
Rūmī asks that prayer not be mixed with the misguided or ostentatious and that worshippers seek divine guidance; Saʿdī urges humility and freedom from the desire for fame.
Actions mixed with ulterior purposes turn from God toward falsehood and lose devotional worth.
Rūmī's lover gives joy, grief, service, and wage to the beloved; seeking another gain is a futile fantasy.
Divine love severs attachment to wealth, children, and life; mature servants do not work for wages but trust the master's generosity.
Al-Sarrī says adorning oneself with good deeds turns them into sins; claiming their value and seeking compensation is worse.
The initial fa links the parable sentence to what precedes it.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: An objection that rain benefits stone by cleaning it is answered by limiting the likeness to the stated feature of loss; al-Qāḍī adds possible benefits of dust.
The parable chooses an outwardly fertile appearance to expose the show-off's deception: bare stone cannot sustain plants even under a thin layer of soil.
The pronoun most naturally refers to the nearest antecedent, the ostentatious spender; another interpretation refers it to the reproachful donor and makes two comparisons.
The pronoun refers to the reproachful donor, so the verse compares him both with the showy spender and with the rain stripped stone.
note: The nearest antecedent favors the showy spender in the competing reading.

view: A report attributes to the Prophet the rule that deeds are judged by intentions.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: A smooth stone's shallow soil looks fertile, but downpour strips it bare: outwardly promising charity proves fruitless at judgment when its motive was show or reproach.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: In the preferred mapping, stone is the hypocritical or reproaching giver, dust is visible work or apparent hope of reward, and rain is Judgment Day, which exposes its lack of sincere roots.
note: Another mapping makes the rain later reproach or ostentation.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: On the later cancellation reading, the stone or gift initially bears real reward, and rain represents subsequent reproach and injury that remove it.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: Dust visibly rests on smooth stone without adhering or sinking in; similarly a gift paired with corrupt intention looks charitable but was never fruitful.
note: This underlies the initial invalidity reading.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: The more precise image is rock concealed beneath seemingly fertile soil until rain uncovers it, rather than soil merely scattered from the rock's top.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: The image works as a composite of promising hope yielding nothing; some also map stone, dust, and rain separately to giver, apparent reward, and ostentation.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: Al-Qaffāl likens deeds to seed: sincere work grows in fertile garden soil, while a reproacher's or hypocrite's seed left on sterile stone gives no crop when needed.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: The barren stone reverses the earlier seed that yields seven hundred grains and contrasts with the fruitful garden of sincere giving.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: The vanishing deed parallels Quranic images of disbelievers' deeds as windblown ashes, scattered dust, or a mirage.

words: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
view: The loss from abusive giving resembles the orchard owner and family whose hopes are destroyed.
Ṣafwān is a large, flat, smooth stone or rock; Arabic also uses ṣafā and ṣafwā for it.
Poetry cited for ṣafwān or related ṣafī describes a smooth stone or stone surface, including lines by Imruʾ al-Qays, Abū Dhuʾayb, and Aws ibn Ḥajar.
Ṣafwān may be treated as a collective noun with singular ṣafwāna; this analysis explains the singular pronoun ʿalayhi.
Ṣafwān may instead be singular, with plural forms reported as ṣafwān, ṣafī, or ṣafiyy.
Al-Mubarrad rejects al-Kisāʾī's ṣafī plural analysis, treating ṣafī as plural of ṣafā; others likewise reject the singular analysis of ṣafwān.
Ṣafwān can be analyzed as a plural of ṣafā, although the faʿlān plural pattern is rare; some prefer this to a singular analysis.
Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī read ṣafwān with fatḥa on the fāʾ, a dialectal but unusual noun form; al-Zaʿrī also vocalizes it thus.
A reported reading vocalizes ṣafwān with fatḥa, with its plural still ṣafwān, analogous to karawān and warshān.
The dust clause describes the stone: either ʿalayhi turāb is a full adjectival clause or ʿalayhi alone modifies the stone and turāb begins a new clause; the latter is preferred by al-Samīn.
Turāb also appears as tū-rāb; related tariba means becoming poor, atraba becoming rich, and turab can mean a same-age peer.
Other related vocabulary includes turāʾib for chest bones and dhā matraba for a poor person sitting in dust.
Aṣāba derives from ṣāba/yaṣūbu; its alif originated as wāw.
Fa-aṣābahu coordinates with the implied verb for dust settled on the stone; its pronoun may return to stone or dust, while the pronoun in fa-tarakahu returns to stone.
Wābil is heavy, abundant, forceful rain, often described as falling in large drops.
The root of wābil also conveys severity or bad consequence, as in severe blows or punishment; Arabic has related verb and adjective forms.
Al-Naḍr orders named rain stages from light spray and drizzle through drops and steady rain to heavy wābil and generous downpour.
Ṣald means bare, smooth, hard, or clean, stripped of soil and unable to grow anything; the image leaves nothing on the stone.
Ṣald also describes a bare or shining bald forehead, sterile ground, an unproductive flint, a miser, or other things devoid of good.
A ṣald or ṣalūd pot is one that boils slowly.
The root ṣald can describe a fire-starter that fails to spark.
Abān ibn Taghlib gives a competing gloss of ṣald as soft stone.
note: Other notes describe the stone as hard.

view: Al-Naqqāsh identifies ṣald or aṣlad as a Hudhayl dialect word for hairless or smooth.
Poetic lines by Ruʾbah, Taʾabbaṭa Sharrā, and Abū Ṭālib attest bare forehead and hard smooth rock senses of ṣald.
Ṣaldan is accusative as the state in which rain left the stone.
Their 'earnings' are what they spent or the deeds performed to acquire a return; spending is called acquisition because they intended to earn reward.
Calling the corrupt givers disbelievers sharply warns believers away from reproach, harm, and ostentation, and explains why the show-off exemplifies disbelief.
The closing description can identify those who die in unbelief; another reading limits the lack of guidance to their present unbelieving state or deeds.
God does not guide disbelievers toward right spending or good while they persist in disbelief or prefer falsehood.
God does not make guidance the recompense for their disbelief.
God does not guide unbelievers to Paradise by their works, or grant them the additional care and success given to believers.
